Que vivent les filles du hood ?: What Are Girls in the Hood Going Through?
Bien qu'elles subissent de graves trauma: Although they suffer serious trauma, their situations are often not taken as seriously as those of boys.
En décembre dernier, La Converse organis: Last December, La Converse held a dialogue evening with young people from Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles on the theme of urban safety. Over our two-hour conversation, we watched people open up: the girls were glad to have a space to speak, and several times the discussion drifted to other topics. Some, however, stayed silent. Maybe, for them, it was still too early to get into deeper things.
C’est à ce moment-là que nous avons déci: That’s when we decided to dig deeper. Aliza Ijaz, a community worker at Prévention Pointe-de-l’Île – the only worker dedicated to girls – knows this reality well. She told us about what she sees every day behind the smiles of girls who say “everything’s fine”: manipulation by boys, delinquency, sexual exploitation… Kingslyne Toussaint, executive director of Équipe RDP, a community social intervention organization, sees the same thing. Both point out that, despite what girls go through in the hood, getting them to talk remains difficult: they are often silenced. And compared with what boys go through, there is a tendency to downplay what some of them have to face every day.

<strong>À Montréal, la sécurité publique: In Montréal, public safety is often approached through the lens of young men. Yet in the borough of Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles, voices we hear too little are rising: those of teenage girls. Last December, at a dialogue evening, we met a group of young girls in RDP–Pointe-aux-Trembles. What are they going through? What is their reality in public space? A report.
Dans l’arrondissement de Rivière-des-Pra: In the borough of Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles, many teenage girls are growing up in a constant climate of insecurity: street harassment, social stigma, pressure from boys, sexual exploitation. Far from being exceptions, these experiences paint a bleak picture of what it means to be female in public space.
« Moi, j’ai été voir la police quand j’a: “I went to the police when I was 15 about a pedophile who wanted to kidnap me. The police officer, she almost laughed in my face,” says Rachelle*, her voice trembling. The memory is still vivid. Behind her testimony, a whole reality takes shape: that of young girls who face harassment and are rarely believed when they dare to speak up.
Regards insistants, remarques déplacées: Insistent stares, inappropriate remarks, hands that come too close – these behaviours, accumulating since childhood, end up creating a permanent climate of aggression. “Nine out of 10 women report having been harassed on the street. And the younger they are, the more they get harassed,” explains Mélusine Dumerchat, a PhD candidate in sociology at the Université du Québec à Montréal.
Pourtant, ces violences quotidiennes son: Yet this everyday violence is most often passed over in silence.
Au Canada, <l1>à peine 5 ou 6 % des agre: In Canada, <l1>barely 5 or 6% of sexual assaults are reported</l1> to police each year. Fear of reprisals, distrust of the police, or the belief that “it won’t lead anywhere” are among the things that stifle voices.
« Ce qui se passe souvent, c’est qu’on o: “What often happens is that girls get forgotten. Because they’re more discreet,” observes Kingslyne Toussaint, executive director of the organization Équipe RDP. And when they do dare to break the silence, they don’t always find a listening ear. “Young women often tell us they aren’t really believed or heard when they report street harassment, when they try to file a complaint, or even when they confide in adults,” adds Mélusine Dumerchat.
Le résultat de tout cela est un sentimen: The result of all this is a feeling of abandonment. Between social indifference and a lack of institutional recognition, victims’ trust is broken and their vulnerability grows.
<strong>Culpabiliser les jeunes filles :: Blaming young girls: “It’s as if public space wasn’t made for them”
« Fais attention à comment tu t’habilles: “Watch how you dress,” “Come home before it gets dark,” “Don’t walk alone.” These instructions, meant to protect, sound like punishments. “Very early on, girls learn that their presence in public space is a risk to be managed,” continues sociologist Mélusine Dumerchat.
À Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembl: In Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles, only one community worker, Aliza Ijaz, is officially dedicated to girls who are vulnerable or at risk of sexual exploitation. For her, the lack of resources has consequences. “There’s nothing to do. And when there’s nothing to do, you try to keep yourself busy… but young people don’t necessarily have the best ways of keeping busy,” she says flatly.
À cela s’ajoute un réseau de transport e: On top of that, there is a public transit network that is still underdeveloped. “It’s hard to get downtown. The bus system isn’t great, the service is infrequent,” she points out. In this context, young girls sometimes depend on boys in the neighbourhood who already have a car.
C’est souvent ainsi que se crée un lien: That is often how a bond of trust is created – before that bond is exploited.
Un des premiers risques auxquels les fil: One of the first risks girls are exposed to is the set-up: staged situations orchestrated by boys in their circle.
Selon l’intervenante, le mécanisme est s: According to the community worker, the mechanism is often the same: “A boy they trust will say: ‘I have a problem with this person; can you message them?’ Since it goes over better coming from a girl, he asks her to go see someone in his place, and then the guy shows up right after in her place.”
« Le problème, c’est que les jeunes fill: “The problem is that young girls, especially at 13 or 14, don’t realize the consequences. They think it’s harmless, almost a joke… but a set-up can easily escalate into a serious assault, even a murder,” the community worker warns.
<strong>« Ce qu’on leur vend, c’est un r: “What they’re sold is a dream, but behind it there’s exploitation”
Toutefois, l’entrée dans l’exploitation: However, entry into sexual exploitation isn’t explained only by the influence of boys, Aliza Ijaz clarifies. Economic reality plays a part too. “The lack of jobs is glaring in Pointe-aux-Trembles. As I said, there aren’t many businesses. Young people have practically no options for work there,” she points out.
Les chiffres parlent d’eux-mêmes : en 20: The numbers speak for themselves: in 2020, more than 2,200 offences related to sexual exploitation were recorded in Quebec, a third of which involved minors. From 2019 to 2022, the number of reported cases doubled.
« Souvent, on parle de jeunes filles de: “Often, we’re talking about girls aged 12 to 17, sometimes up to 25. They’re still in school, they don’t work. But on social media, you have to look the part: have the nails, the bag, the car… That costs money. So they’re tempted to find a quick option: commit petty offences, sell their bodies, answer the call of someone older,” she explains.
D’autres se retrouvent impliquées dans d: Others end up involved in major offences, knowing that the sentences reserved for them are often lighter than those of their male accomplices. <l1>According to Public Safety Canada’s 2023 annual report on the correctional system and conditional release</l1>, teenage girls are far less often sent behind bars than boys. In 2022–2023, only 2.9% of them received a custodial sentence, compared with 8.2% of boys.
Au fil du temps, certaines adolescentes: Over time, some teenage girls become go-betweens for rival criminal groups, gaining the trust of both sides and unwittingly orchestrating violent confrontations. “They end up caught between two clans. They know too much, they become visible, threatened. Even when they want to get out, they’re afraid: their address, their family, their school are known,” explains the executive director of Équipe RDP.
Aliza Ijaz, elle, insiste : « Ces filles: Aliza Ijaz insists: “These girls live in fear and accumulate trauma. They’re used, but because they don’t die at the end of the story – unlike boys involved in gun violence and organized crime – their situation isn’t taken seriously. It’s judged to be ‘merely’ sexual exploitation. Yet these wounds mark them for life. I consider it just as serious. But in the media, it’s not seen that way.”
<strong>« Il ne suffit pas de promettre: “It’s not enough to promise to act, you have to actually do it”
Aujourd’hui, les jeunes filles que nous: Today, the young girls we met want to “come forward.” Gathered at our dialogue evening, they speak out, they want to occupy public space and make known what they go through. But they also know that solutions have to come from decision-makers. “It’s not enough to promise to act, you have to actually do it,” insists one of them. Normalizing these conversations, talking about them more, adapting interventions: these are the first steps toward a society where girls can walk in public space without fear.
Elles expriment également le besoin d’av: They also express the need for activities designed for them. “I feel more comfortable when there are more girls. I’d like to do activities with just them, that way I could open up,” says another. Then a third adds: “I feel safer with girls, for sure. We don’t only want mixed activities, but also times reserved for girls, like henna…”
Pour Jessey Charles, intervenante d’Équi: For Jessey Charles, a community worker at Équipe RDP, these spaces must go even further: “We need to think about activities that highlight girls, that build their self-esteem. And also put them in touch with women who have succeeded in fields often associated with boys, like politics, medicine or science.”
Aliza conclut : « Il faut écouter ce que: Aliza concludes: “We have to listen to what girls have to say and go further to understand their reality. We have to keep pushing, without letting go, so that what they’ve lived is exposed. Even a small step forward can make a difference. Tomorrow, the effects could be much greater.”

La comparaison avec les garçons est frap: The contrast with boys is striking. “At home, they always told me, ‘What will people think if they see you outside?’” says one of the girls at the dialogue evening. “It’s as if public space wasn’t made for them,” M<sup>s</sup> Dumerchat stresses.
Au-delà d’un cadre familial qui limitera: Beyond a family setting that may already limit their presence outdoors, girls in Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles run into another problem: a lack of spaces suited to them. “There aren’t many safe places for girls in the east end. You can tell they’d like to go to a shopping mall, to cafés… Unfortunately, it’s really empty [in the east end of Montréal],” M<sup>s</sup> Toussaint laments.
Même les espaces communautaires ne sembl: Even community spaces don’t seem to be designed for them. “They don’t feel comfortable going to community organizations. At the youth centre, for example, there are apparently too many guys, so the girls don’t go. Our activities, unfortunately, also mostly bring in boys, because we work with a lot of marginalized youth, who are mostly guys,” M<sup>s</sup> Toussaint acknowledges.
« Il a une voiture, ça semble intéressan:
“He has a car, that seems interesting. He’s someone your age, you think there’s nothing wrong with it,” M<sup>s</sup> Ijaz describes. “But that relationship of trust can quickly shift:
that person will bring you to other people, or maybe persuade you to go down a path you didn’t expect: ‘I’ve got money, I’ve got a car… and I can show you how to get some too.’”
« Malheureusement, même si on parle ici: “Unfortunately, even though we’re talking about girls here, boys are always involved,” M<sup>s</sup> Ijaz continues. “They use girls a lot in their conflicts. And sometimes that pulls them toward crime, substance use, then sexual exploitation…”
Pour une adolescente, ça peut sembler bé: For a teenage girl, it can seem harmless: “He’s my friend, he asked me to do it, so I do it,” she might tell herself. But very quickly, these favours become increasingly risky “favours”… Presented as ordinary, these requests can quickly tip into sexual exploitation. “It happens in small steps… The boy will first ask the girl to go spend the evening with someone else. And then it could go further… until the day someone tells you, ‘If you sleep with him, you can help me wipe out a debt,’” M<sup>s</sup> Ijaz explains.
Et pour Kingslyne Toussaint, directrice: And for Kingslyne Toussaint, director of Équipe RDP, social media also amplifies this process. Some teenage girls see “glamorous” lifestyles there: luxury bags, big cars, nails and hair always flawless. But if you have neither a steady job nor financial independence, those ideals are out of reach. “What they’re being sold is a dream, but behind it there’s exploitation,” M<sup>s</sup> Toussaint points out.
« On voit maintenant des jeunes filles d: “We’re now seeing girls aged 15 to 22 directly involved in offences like car theft. It’s not seen as gun violence, but it’s part of it, because those vehicles are often used afterward to commit crimes. Girls are recruited for these offences because the sentences are lighter: community service, most often,” M<sup>s</sup> Toussaint says. The same study confirms this trend: in 2021-2022, 3.8% of convicted teenage girls received this type of sentence, compared with 1.9% of boys. And the gap persisted the following year: 3.6% of girls, compared with 2.6% of boys.
Elle reconnaît tout de même que la libér: She acknowledges, however, that speaking out doesn’t come easily. “For a girl’s story to be told, she often has to agree to testify publicly, there has to be an investigation, twists and turns. But going to the police after suffering abuse, even ‘minor’ abuse, can already destroy you forever. And too often, it goes no further,” M<sup>s</sup> Ijaz says flatly.
Voilà pourquoi la prévention est essenti: That’s why prevention is essential. “We try to make them understand that there’s no such thing as a ‘small crime,’” M<sup>s</sup> Toussaint insists. “Every act tightens the cycle and makes getting out harder.”
